reason: The text explicitly demonstrates and reinforces social hierarchy throughout. Naomi consistently gives directives to Ruth as her mother-in-law; Boaz maintains clear authority over his servants and workers, issuing commands that are obeyed (וַיְצַו֩ בֹּ֨עַז אֶת־ נְעָרָ֜יו); the narrative describes familial hierarchy (husband/wife relationships), economic hierarchy (master/servant), legal hierarchy (elders at the gate as judicial authorities), and gender hierarchy (patriarchal structure with male authority and female dependence). The redemption law (ge'ullah) operates within a framework of formal social hierarchy and property rights. Ruth's exceptional kindness does not challenge hierarchy but rather demonstrates proper hierarchical conduct—the powerful caring for the vulnerable within an established social order. There is no textual evidence suggesting hierarchy is unimportant or discouraged; rather, it is the foundational organizing principle throughout.
